spark.summary: Idempotency keys and deduplication logs ensure that network retries, at-least-once message deliveries, and double-clicks execute state mutations at most once while returning the original cached outcome.
spark.keyTakeaway: Because distributed networks only guarantee at-least-once delivery, every mutating API and consumer must pair a client-generated idempotency key with an atomic database/transaction check—not a separate read-then-write.

concept.whyItMatters: In distributed systems, timeouts are ambiguous: when a client or Kafka consumer times out waiting for an ACK, it cannot tell whether the server crashed before processing or after committing. Retrying without idempotency double-charges credit cards, mints duplicate orders, or corrupts inventory balances. Combining client-supplied `Idempotency-Key` headers (or event IDs) with atomic persistence turns at-least-once transport into effectively-once business effects.
whenToUse: Payment, billing, and ledger APIs (e.g., Stripe-style `POST /v1/charges` with `Idempotency-Key` UUIDv4) where duplicate execution causes financial loss.
Event-driven consumers reading from at-least-once brokers (Kafka, SQS Standard, SNS, RabbitMQ) that redeliver messages on consumer rebalance or visibility timeout expiry.
Mobile or flaky-network clients that automatically retry timed-out POST/PATCH requests.
whenNotToUse: Naturally idempotent operations (`PUT /users/42` full replacement, `DELETE /sessions/9`, or `SET status = 'PAID'`) where re-running yields the identical state without side-effect logs.
Read-only `GET`/`HEAD` endpoints that perform no mutations.
High-throughput fire-and-forget telemetry/metrics where storing a deduplication key per event costs more than the 0.01% duplicate rate.
keyPoints: Idempotency is an end-to-end property: the client generates a unique key (UUIDv4) *before* the first attempt and reuses that exact key across all retries of the same logical operation.

Always validate a payload hash (e.g., SHA-256 of request body) alongside the key; reusing the same `Idempotency-Key` with a different amount or target must return `422 Unprocessable Entity` / `409 Conflict`.

Atomic state transitions are mandatory: insert the key (`INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` or DynamoDB `attribute_not_exists(pk)`) inside the same DB transaction as the business write, or use a Redis `SET NX EX` lock with an explicit `IN_PROGRESS` state.

Concurrent duplicate requests arriving while the first is still `IN_PROGRESS` should return `409 Conflict` (or `425 Too Early` with `Retry-After`) rather than running in parallel or returning an empty response.

Kafka's `enable.idempotence=true` deduplicates *broker-level* producer retries via `(PID, SequenceNumber)`, and transactional outbox + consumer-side `processed_events` tables deduplicate *application-level* side effects.

examples.title: Stripe-Pattern Payment Charge API in PostgreSQL
examples.scenario: A mobile checkout app sends `POST /v1/payments` (`amount=4999`, `Idempotency-Key: 9b1deb4d-...`). The gateway times out at 3s due to a slow 3DS bank call and retries 2 seconds later while the first request is still running, then retries a third time after it commits.
examples.outcome: Attempt 1 inserts `(key, payload_hash, status='IN_PROGRESS')` in Postgres. Attempt 2 hits the unique key while `IN_PROGRESS` and receives `409 Conflict` (`Retry-After: 2`). Attempt 1 commits the ledger row and updates the idempotency record to `status='COMPLETED', response_code=201, response_body=...`. Attempt 3 reads the completed record and replays the exact `201 Created` JSON without charging the card again.

examples.title: Kafka Consumer Deduplication via Atomic Processed-Events Table
examples.scenario: An order-fulfillment consumer reads `OrderPaid` events from Kafka (`at-least-once`). After updating inventory in Postgres for `event_id=evt_8821`, the consumer crashes before committing its Kafka offset, causing a rebalance and redelivery of `evt_8821`.
examples.outcome: Inside a single Postgres transaction, the consumer executes `INSERT INTO processed_events(event_id) VALUES ('evt_8821') ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`. On redelivery, `rowcount == 0`, so the consumer skips the inventory decrement and commits the Kafka offset cleanly.

tradeOffs.factor: Same-DB Transaction vs. Redis Dedup Cache
tradeOffs.pro: Inserting the dedup key in the same ACID transaction as the business mutation guarantees zero split-brain between state and dedup record.
tradeOffs.con: Adds write IOPS and storage growth to the primary OLTP database, requiring TTL partitioning/pruning (e.g., 24h–7d retention).

tradeOffs.factor: Strict In-Progress Locking vs. Optimistic Parallelism
tradeOffs.pro: Returning `409` on concurrent duplicate keys prevents race conditions and duplicate external API calls (e.g., to Stripe/Adyen).
tradeOffs.con: If the worker holding `IN_PROGRESS` crashes without a lease timeout, the key stays locked until TTL expiry unless a lease/heartbeat or recovery state machine is implemented.

tradeOffs.factor: Dedup Retention Window vs. Storage Cost
tradeOffs.pro: Longer retention (e.g., 7–30 days) protects against delayed batch retries and dead-letter queue (DLQ) replays.
tradeOffs.con: Keeping millions of UUID keys and cached JSON responses bloats indexes unless stored in time-partitioned tables or DynamoDB TTL items.

failureModes.name: Check-Then-Act Race Condition
failureModes.description: Two identical retries simultaneously execute `SELECT * FROM idempotency WHERE key = ?`, both see `NULL`, and both execute the payment charge before either writes the key.
failureModes.mitigation: Use an atomic `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` / `UNIQUE` constraint or Redis `SET key value NX EX 3600`—never a separate `SELECT` followed by `INSERT`.

failureModes.name: Dual-Write Split-Brain (Redis + Postgres)
failureModes.description: The service writes the business row to Postgres and then crashes before writing the dedup key to Redis (or writes Redis first and Postgres rolls back), causing either a missed dedup or a permanently blocked key.
failureModes.mitigation: Keep the idempotency/processed_events table in the same ACID database as the business mutation, or use the Transactional Outbox pattern.

failureModes.name: Orphaned IN_PROGRESS Lock After Worker Crash
failureModes.description: A worker sets `status='IN_PROGRESS'` and is OOM-killed mid-request; every subsequent client retry gets `409 Conflict` forever.
failureModes.mitigation: Attach a short lease timestamp (`locked_until = now() + 30s`) to `IN_PROGRESS` records—if expired and no external side effect was started, allow safe takeover or query the downstream provider by the same idempotency key.

failureModes.name: Key Reuse with Mutated Payload
failureModes.description: A buggy client hardcodes an `Idempotency-Key` across two different orders ($10 then $500) and silently receives the cached $10 response.
failureModes.mitigation: Store `request_hash = SHA256(method + path + canonical_body)` with the key and reject mismatches with `422 Unprocessable Entity`.

commonMistakes: Generating the idempotency key on the server instead of the client—server-generated keys cannot detect client network retries.
Implementing deduplication with a non-atomic `GET` followed by `SET` or `SELECT` followed by `INSERT`.
Forgetting to pass the idempotency key downstream to external payment gateways or webhooks, causing duplicate external calls on internal retries.
Omitting payload-hash verification, allowing accidental key reuse to return a stale response for a different request.
Using `SETNX` in Redis without an expiration (`EX`), leaking memory indefinitely until eviction.

sections.content:
## The idea

In an unreliable network, **at-least-once delivery** is the practical baseline: HTTP clients retry on `504`/timeout, and message brokers (Kafka, SQS) redeliver unacknowledged events after consumer crashes. Without protection, retrying a non-idempotent operation like `POST /transfers` or `decrement_stock` executes the side effect multiple times.

**Idempotency** means applying an operation multiple times produces the same system state and observable result as applying it once. For naturally non-idempotent operations (creating a charge, appending a ledger entry), we achieve this via an **idempotency key** (client-generated UUIDv4) or **message ID** paired with an atomic deduplication store.

The core pattern has three phases: (1) **Acquire** the key atomically (`IN_PROGRESS` + payload hash), (2) **Execute** the business mutation and persist the serialized response inside the same ACID boundary (or atomic state machine), and (3) **Replay** the stored response on any subsequent retry with the same key.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace `POST /v1/transfers` (`amount=25000`, `to='acct_88'`, `Idempotency-Key: 7c9e6679-7425-40de-944b-e07fc1f90ae7`):

1. **Request 1 (Initial)**: The API computes `req_hash = SHA256(canonical_json)`. Inside a Postgres transaction, it runs `INSERT INTO idempotency_keys(key, req_hash, status, locked_until) VALUES ($1, $2, 'IN_PROGRESS', now() + interval '30 seconds') ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING`. It inserts 1 row and commits the lock.
2. **Request 2 (Concurrent Retry at +1.2s)**: The mobile client timed out at 1s and retries with the same key. `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` inserts 0 rows. The server selects the existing row, verifies `req_hash` matches, sees `status = 'IN_PROGRESS'` with `locked_until > now()`, and immediately returns `409 Conflict` with `Retry-After: 2`.
3. **Completion of Request 1 (+2.4s)**: After debiting the sender and crediting `acct_88` inside a single DB transaction, the server updates `idempotency_keys` in that same commit: `status = 'COMPLETED', response_code = 201, response_body = '{"transfer_id":"tr_501"}'`. 
4. **Request 3 (Post-Commit Retry at +3.5s)**: The client retries once more. The server finds `status = 'COMPLETED'` and returns the exact cached `201 Created` JSON (`{"transfer_id":"tr_501"}`) in 2 ms without touching the ledger.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Messaging deduplication: Kafka, SQS, and the Outbox pattern
sections.content:
## Messaging deduplication: Kafka, SQS, and the Outbox pattern

API idempotency is only half the story; asynchronous pipelines need two additional layers:

- **Producer-to-Broker**: Kafka's `enable.idempotence=true` assigns every producer a `ProducerID` (`PID`) and monotonic `SequenceNumber` per partition, so broker-level retries on network blips are deduplicated before appending to the log. AWS SQS FIFO offers a 5-minute `MessageDeduplicationId` window.
- **Broker-to-Consumer**: Neither Kafka's idempotent producer nor SQS prevents a consumer from processing a message twice after a crash before offset commit/delete. Consumers must maintain a `processed_events(event_id PRIMARY KEY, processed_at)` table in the same database as their state updates and check/insert it inside the same transaction.
- **Transactional Outbox**: When an API must update Postgres *and* publish a Kafka event, write the event to an `outbox` table in the same Postgres transaction and let Debezium (CDC) or a poller publish it—giving the event a deterministic `event_id` for downstream consumers.

## Deduplication implementation comparison

| Approach | Atomicity Guarantee | Concurrency Handling | Best Suited For | Main Limitation |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Same-DB `idempotency_keys` Table** | Full ACID with business write | `ON CONFLICT` + `IN_PROGRESS` lease (`409`) | Payments, orders, ledger APIs | Adds OLTP storage; needs TTL pruning |
| **Redis `SET NX EX` + Cache** | Separate from SQL DB (risk of split-brain) | Atomic lock via Lua / `SET NX` | High-QPS soft dedup, rate/click guards | Lost on Redis failover unless RDB/AOF + DB backup |
| **Consumer `processed_events` Table** | Full ACID with consumer state update | `PRIMARY KEY` violation skips duplicate | Kafka / SQS / RabbitMQ consumers | Only protects single-DB consumers |
| **SQS FIFO `MessageDeduplicationId`** | Broker-enforced 5-min window | Drops duplicate enqueue attempts | Short-window task queues | 5-minute hard cap; doesn't cover consumer crashes |

## Failure modes

- **External side-effect split-brain**: Calling a third-party API (e.g., Stripe) *inside* a Postgres transaction that later rolls back leaves an external charge with no local DB record. Instead, pass the same `Idempotency-Key` to Stripe, commit a `PENDING_EXTERNAL` state first, call Stripe outside the DB lock, then finalize.
- **Expired dedup window on DLQ replay**: If `idempotency_keys` is pruned after 24 hours, replaying a 3-day-old dead-letter queue batch re-executes old mutations.
- **Unbounded table growth**: Storing full 50 KB response bodies for 10M requests/day adds 500 GB/day; use daily range partitions (`DROP TABLE` instead of `DELETE`) and cap cached body sizes.
- **Leased lock starvation**: Setting `locked_until` to 10 minutes on a 2-second endpoint traps clients in `409` loops after a single pod crash.

## Key design & retention rules

1. **Scope keys per tenant/user**: Key the unique constraint on `(tenant_id, idempotency_key)` so Tenant A cannot collide with or probe Tenant B's keys.
2. **Keep `IN_PROGRESS` leases tight**: Set `locked_until` to `2x–3x` the endpoint's p99 timeout (e.g., 15–30 seconds).
3. **Partition by time**: Use Postgres declarative daily partitions or DynamoDB `ttl` attributes (24–72 hours for APIs, 7–30 days for async `processed_events`) to drop expired keys with zero vacuum overhead.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Require client-generated UUIDv4 `Idempotency-Key` headers on all non-idempotent `POST`/`PATCH` endpoints.
- [ ] Scope uniqueness to `(tenant_id, key)` and verify `SHA-256(request_body)` matches (`422` on mismatch).
- [ ] Acquire `IN_PROGRESS` atomically (`INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` or `SET NX EX`) with a bounded lease timeout.
- [ ] Commit the business mutation and cached response in the same ACID transaction.
- [ ] Propagate the idempotency key to downstream webhooks and payment providers.
- [ ] Pair at-least-once consumers with a `processed_events` table and time-partitioned TTL cleanup.

interviewProblems.title: Idempotency & Message Deduplication
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Idempotency & Message Deduplication. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Idempotency keys and deduplication logs ensure that network retries, at-least-once message deliveries, and double-clicks execute state mutations at most once while returning the original cached outcome.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Payment / Order API applies the primary invariant and coordinates with ACID Ledger + Dedup DB.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, ACID Ledger + Dedup DB experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Use an atomic `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` / `UNIQUE` constraint or Redis `SET key value NX EX 3600`—never a separate `SELECT` followed by `INSERT`.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Because distributed networks only guarantee at-least-once delivery, every mutating API and consumer must pair a client-generated idempotency key with an atomic database/transaction check—not a separate read-then-write.
Avoid trap: Generating the idempotency key on the server instead of the client—server-generated keys cannot detect client network retries.
Avoid trap: Implementing deduplication with a non-atomic `GET` followed by `SET` or `SELECT` followed by `INSERT`.
When to reach for it: Payment, billing, and ledger APIs (e.g., Stripe-style `POST /v1/charges` with `Idempotency-Key` UUIDv4) where duplicate execution causes financial loss.
When to reach for it: Event-driven consumers reading from at-least-once brokers (Kafka, SQS Standard, SNS, RabbitMQ) that redeliver messages on consumer rebalance or visibility timeout expiry.

putItTogether.title: Putting Idempotency And Deduplication Together
putItTogether.summary: Because distributed networks only guarantee at-least-once delivery, every mutating API and consumer must pair a client-generated idempotency key with an atomic database/transaction check—not a separate read-then-write.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Idempotency And Deduplication before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Attempt 1 inserts `(key, payload_hash, status='IN_PROGRESS')` in Postgres. Attempt 2 hits the unique key while `IN_PROGRESS` and receives `409 Conflict` (`Retry-After: 2`). Attempt 1 commits the ledger row and updates the idempotency record to `status='COMPLETED', response_code=201, response_body=...`. Attempt 3 reads the completed record and replays the exact `201 Created` JSON without charging the card again.
